newsitem.title: USA: Chip stocks rise after book-to-bill report.
newsitem.headline: Chip stocks rise after book-to-bill report.

text.p: Computer chip stocks rallied Wednesday after a report that a key gauge of chip demand rose to the highest level of the year in September, a sign the industry's worst days may be behind it.

The gains were broad, with Texas Instruments adding $1.875 to $57 on the New York Stock Exchange, and Cirrus Logic Inc., a maker of speciality chips for personal computers, up $1.75 to $22.125 on Nasdaq.
The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index, a basket of semiconductor stocks, jumped 5.35 points to 195.65, a gain of 2.8 percent.

The Semiconductor Industry Association said on Tuesday that its book-to-bill ratio rose to 0.99 in September from 0.93 in August. The ratio means chip makers received $99 in new orders last month for every $100 in chips they sold.

"The month of September was explosive from a PC order standpoint, literally explosive," said analyst Charles Boucher at UBS Securities, adding that much of the gain in the book-to-bill data was from orders for PC-related chips.
The association said orders jumped 9 percent to $3.19 billion in September while sales rose 2.1 percent to $3.22 billion, the first rise this year.
"That 9 percent was a real surprise," Boucher said.
John Lazlo of PaineWebber said he expects growing PC sales to lead to steady increases in chip orders and sales through the rest of 1996.
The report seemed to confirm that the industry has bottomed out and is poised to see a rebound in profits, perhaps as early as the fourth quarter, analysts said.

Still, some analysts said chip producers were unlikely to see a return to the heady days of 1994 and 1995, when strong demand for PCs fuelled a shortage of memory chips and pushed prices -- and chip makers' earnings -- sharply higher.

Chip stocks have rallied in recent weeks on early signs of a rebound in the industry. Slower PC sales and a rush of new chip capacity, especially in Asia, led to lower chip sales and tumbling prices earlier in the year.

But the rally gained momentum after the book-to-bill report pointed to a halt in the freefall of memory chip prices, analysts said. The gains came despite weakness in other high-technology issues and the broader market.

National Semiconductor added 87.5 cents to $20.75 on the NYSE, and Atmel jumped $1.625 to $34.125 and Applied Materials, which makes fabrication equipment for chip producers, added $1.25 to $29.25, both on Nasdaq.
Lazlo said that some chip stocks skipped Wednesday's rally, notably Intel Corp., the world's largest chipmaker, since it has risen steadily for two months. Intel lost 75 cents to $100.875 on Nasdaq.
"Keep in mind these stocks have outperformed the market over the past two months," Lazlo said.
Prices of memory chips fell to about one-sixth of their January prices but in mid-September that stopped, and prices have even inched up a bit, analysts said.

Since memory chips make up about 40 percent of the unit volume of industry-wide chip sales, the falling prices were a big reason that orders and the book-to-bill ratio were weak all year, Montgomery Securities analyst Jon Joseph said.
